interactive.title: Two machines in a chain
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on chaining two functions. Two machines sit in a row, each a box with its rule written inside, joined by a short pipe. Drag an input into the first box: its output rides along the join, where the middle value is shown, into the second box, and the second box's output drops out at the end. A switch swaps the two boxes, and the rule above them rewrites between f(g(x)) and g(f(x)). The opening chain is g, add 4, then f, double: 3 becomes 7 on the join and 14 comes out. Swapped, 3 is doubled to 6 on the join and then 4 is added, giving 10. The two answers differ by 4 because a 4 added first goes through the doubler too and becomes 8, while a 4 added last stays 4. f(g(x)) is said 'f of g of x' and is worked from the inside bracket out, so g goes first. Lesson 1's machine, × 3 then − 1, comes back as two boxes: 5 gives 15 on the join and 14 out, and swapped it gives 4 and then 12. Then the flow meter from lessons 3 and 4. The first box is the controller's straight-line rule d(I) = (I − 4) ÷ 16, which takes off the 4 mA at the bottom of the loop and divides by the 16 mA span to give the fraction of full pressure difference. The second box is Q(d) = √d, the fraction of full flow, because the pressure difference goes as the square of the flow. 12 mA gives 0.5 on the join and 0.707 out, 71% flow, and 8 mA gives 0.25 and then 0.5, 50% flow. A third box then adds a second square root, as when the transmitter and the controller both take it, though it belongs in one or the other but not both: 12 mA reads 0.841, 84%, and 8 mA reads 71%. A screen chains 'take 4, then square root': an input of 2 puts −2 on the join and the root box answers 'no value', so the chain takes only inputs of 4 and up. Swapped, the root comes first and refuses every negative input instead, such as −4. The last puzzle chains g(x) = x − 3 and f(x) = x², and f(g(5)) = 4 is lesson 5's point (5, 4) on the square slid 3 right: lesson 5's shifts were chains all along. UK books also write f(g(x)) as fg(x), with g still first. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick shows the slip that makes it, such as working the outside machine first, stopping at the join, squaring instead of rooting, or taking the root twice.
interactive.ignores: The boxes pass one number at a time, a step at a time; a real controller works on its signal all the time. The machines are exact: real transmitters and meters carry small errors, and the flow meter is drawn as its ideal square-law rule. Flow is shown as a fraction of full flow; turning it into litres a minute would be one more box in the chain, multiplying by the meter's full-scale flow. Some installations take the square root in the transmitter instead of the controller, which is the same chain with that box in a different place, still with one root. The add 4, double, take 3 and take 4 machines and the 8 and 16 mA readings are example values. Only ordinary (real) numbers are used.

explain.text:
A chain of two functions feeds the output of the first machine straight in as the input of the second.[^2] The order you join them in matters, because the second machine works on whatever the first one hands it. Swap them round and the same input usually gives a different output.

Take g, which adds 4, and f, which doubles. Put 3 into g and 7 comes out. That 7 is f's input, so 14 drops out. Swap them and 3 is doubled to 6 first, then 4 is added, giving 10. The machines are the same, so the difference comes from the 4. Added first, it goes through the doubler too and becomes 8; added last, it stays 4. That is the 4 between 14 and 10. Two machines that both only add, or both only multiply, give the same either way, so a swap usually changes the answer, but not always. Textbooks write the first chain as f(g(x)), said "f of g of x". As with any bracket, the inside is worked first: g(x) is found, then fed into f. So f(g(3)) = f(7) = 14, while g(f(3)) = g(6) = 10. UK books often write it fg(x): g(x) is still found first, then put into f.[^7] A function built from a chain like this is called a [[composite function]], and the SQA HN engineering maths unit includes working them out.[^3]

The flow meter from lessons 3 and 4 is a chain of two machines. The controller's first machine turns the loop's mA into a fraction of full pressure difference with a straight-line rule,[^4] d(I) = (I − 4) ÷ 16: take off the 4 mA at the bottom of the loop, then divide by the 16 mA span. The pressure difference goes as the square of the flow, so the second machine takes the square root to give the fraction of full flow,[^5] Q(d) = √d. At 12 mA, d(12) = 8 ÷ 16 = 0.5 on the join, and Q(0.5) = 0.707 comes out: 50% pressure difference, but 71% flow.[^1] The square root is taken in the transmitter or in the controller, but not both.[^8] If both take it, 0.707 goes into a second root and 0.841 comes out, so the controller shows 84% for a 71% flow. Each machine belongs in the chain once. Lesson 8 shows why d is lesson 2's rule run backwards, giving a fraction instead of a percentage.

Each machine must also take what the one before hands it. Lesson 4's square root has no value for a negative input,[^6] so in the chain "take 4, then square root" an input of 2 puts −2 on the join and the chain gives no value. It takes only inputs of 4 and up. Lesson 5's slides were chains as well: x² + 3 is "square, then add 3", and (x − 3)² is "take 3, then square". **In a chain f(g(x)), g's output becomes f's input,[^2] so the order you join them in decides what comes out, and swapping it usually changes the answer.**

analogy.text: Think of stripping a cable and then crimping a lug onto it. The crimper works on whatever the stripper hands it, a bared end, so the first job's output is the second job's input. Swap the order and the crimper is handed a different input, the insulated end, and you get a different result.
analogy.breaks: A crimp onto insulation is a failed joint, while a swapped chain of functions usually still gives a number, just a different one. But a swap can also change whether there is an answer at all: "take 4, then square root" has no value at 2, while with the root first 2 gives −2.59. And some pairs of machines, such as two that only add, give the same result in either order, as some jobs on a cable can be done either way round.

practice.text:
- Find the inside machine. In f(g(x)) it is g, so g goes first.
- Put the input into g and write down the middle value.
- Check the outside machine takes that value: no square root of a negative number, no dividing by zero.
- Put the middle value into f. What comes out is f(g(x)).
- If the order is in doubt, run one number through both ways. Different answers mean the order matters for this pair.

**Rule of thumb:** Inside first, as with any bracket. The machine written nearest the x works first.

**Worked example:** A flow loop reads 16 mA. First machine: d(16) = (16 − 4) ÷ 16 = 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75, so 75% of full pressure difference. Second machine: Q(0.75) = √0.75 = 0.866, so about 87% of full flow. Check: 0.866 × 0.866 comes back to 0.75, near enough, so the root is right.

**Mistakes to watch for**
- Working the outside machine first. With f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 4, f(g(2)) = 12, but doubling first gives g(f(2)) = 8.
- Stopping at the join. The middle value, 0.5 at 12 mA, is the pressure difference, not the flow.
- Taking the root twice. At 12 mA the flow is 71%, but a second root would read 84%.
- Feeding a machine a value it refuses. "Take 4, then square root" has no value at 2.

checks.label: The process of combining functions so that the output of one function becomes the input of another: on every screen and after every answer, each number drawn on a join or at the output is what its box makes of the number before it
√0.5 = 0.707, so a 12 mA signal from the DP cell is 50% DP but 71% flow rate: the flow meter screen puts 0.5 on the join for 12 mA and 0.707, 71% of full flow, drops out

The DP is proportional to the square of the flow, so the system scales flow from the square root of the DP: squaring what Q gives brings back the pressure difference at every reading from 4 to 20 mA, while squaring instead of rooting gives 0.0625 at 8 mA, not 0.5

The square root for DP-based flow can be taken either in the transmitter or in the controller (but not both): with the root taken in both, the third box turns 12 mA's true 0.707 into 0.841, so the screen reads 84%, and 8 mA's 50% reads 71%
fg(x) is calculated by finding g(x) first, and then substituting this into the function f: the f of g of x screen runs g first, 3 to 7 on the join, then f, 14 out, under f(g(x))

Each value is converted with the linear equation y = mx + b: d(I) = (I − 4) ÷ 16 is a straight line, 0 at the 4 mA bottom of the loop and 1 at 20 mA across the 16 mA span, rising the same 1/16 for every 1 mA

The domain leaves out any input that would mean taking the square root of a negative number: take 4 then square root gives no value for every input tried below 4 and a value from 4 up, while root first refuses every negative input and takes 0, 1 and 2

Every worked number is right (7 and 14 from 3; 9 and 18 from 5, 14 doubling first; 6 and 10 swapped; 15 and 14, swapped 4 and 12; f(g(2)) = 12, g(f(2)) = 8; 0.5, 0.707, 71% at 12 mA; 0.25, 0.5, 50% at 8 mA, 0.0625 squared; two roots 84% and 71%; −2 then no value; root first −4 refused, 1 gives −3, 2 gives 1.41 then −2.59; 2 and 4 from 5, 22 squaring first; 16 mA gives 0.75 and 0.866, 87%), and every line of working drawn says so

A swap usually changes the answer, but not always: from 3, add 4 then double gives 14 and double then add 4 gives 10, the 4 added first being doubled to 8; the switch redraws the rule line, f(g(x)) to g(f(x)); two machines that both only add, or both only multiply, agree either way

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, and after each wrong pick the picture shows the slip making exactly that answer: the outside machine first, stopping at the join, squaring instead of rooting, the first order's answer, or an input the root takes
Before an answer, nothing in a puzzle's picture gives it away: the joins and the output wait as question marks, or show only the first order's run
Every demonstration has settled within 4.6 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends, and every swap within 4 s; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 3 s
